title: The Path of Truth
intro: Abd al-Rahman al-Sa'di answers someone asking how to follow the people of right guidance. In his commentary, Abd al-Razzaq al-Badr takes the title The Path of Truth from the opening and records that one of his two manuscript copies was written in 1345 AH. The sixty-five verses pass from belief in God, the messengers and resurrection to what a person can see in the night sky and in the self. After counsel on patience and friendship, al-Sa'di devotes the close to remembrance, drawing on the Prophet’s advice to Mu'adh and on images of a race, a planting and a tongue kept moist.

translation: You who ask about the path of truth and seek
to walk the people’s way in earnest and find happiness,
1.sharh: The poem opens in the middle of a conversation. The questioner already has a destination in mind and needs to know how to get there.

translation: consider what I have put into verse, may God guide you,
as one who means to reach the truth.
2.sharh: The prayer for guidance briefly interrupts the instruction. How one reads matters to the teacher as much as the words being read.

translation: We acknowledge God. There is no Lord besides Him,
a God glorified upon the mighty Throne.
3.sharh: The teacher begins the declaration in the first person plural. God’s sole lordship and the image of the Throne precede the account of how people worship.

translation: We bear witness that God is the One we worship,
the One we single out in humble love.
4.sharh: Worship here brings together affection and submission. Singling God out applies to that worshipful love.

translation: To God belong all praise, glory and acclaim.
That is why all turn to God.
5.sharh: Turning to God follows from the opening claim about praise. The passage joins what is admirable in God to the impulse to seek Him.

translation: The angels, earth and heaven proclaim His glory.
All creation truly glorifies and praises Him.
6.sharh: The list includes the earth and sky themselves. It recalls the Quranic description of everything praising God, even where human beings cannot understand its praise.

translation: He is above any rival or matching equal,
above the attributes of the deficient. Exalted is the One.
7.sharh: The first half rules out an equal. The second asks what would follow from treating God like a creature subject to limits.

translation: We affirm all reports of His attributes
and disown the readings of those who deny them.
8.sharh: Al-Sa'di states his approach to scriptural language about God. The interpretation he objects to is one he regards as emptying a divine attribute of its meaning.

translation: The mind cannot encompass the nature of His attributes.
Accept what Muhammad, the Messenger, said.
9.sharh: He distinguishes recognising an attribute from knowing precisely how it is true of God. The word translated as nature points to that innermost reality.

translation: He is the One sought by all, exalted in His attributes.
Every creature turns to God in need.
10.sharh: The divine name al-Samad and the verb for seeking someone out share a root. Human dependence explains the name in the second half.

translation: He is Most High in being, rank and power,
near, answering, showing affection to His creatures.
11.sharh: For al-Sa'di divine transcendence and responsiveness can be affirmed together. The one whose rule stands above all is the one near enough to answer.

translation: He is the Living, the Sustainer, generous and self-sufficient.
Every praiseworthy attribute is ascribed to God.
12.sharh: The Sustainer both subsists of Himself and sustains others. His gifts therefore come from One who does not depend on their recipients.

translation: His knowledge and power encompass all creation,
as do His kindness and goodness. Him alone we worship.
13.sharh: The verb “encompass” governs kindness as well as knowledge and power. The resulting profession recalls the opening chapter of the Quran.

translation: He sees every speck in all the worlds.
He hears His servants’ voices and is witness.
14.sharh: The scale moves down to a speck and out to all human voices. The final verb gives this knowledge the immediacy of a witness’s presence.

translation: His is the kingdom, and praise encompassing His whole realm.
Creation bears witness to His supreme wisdom.
15.sharh: Sovereignty explains who rules the entire domain. Praise and wisdom explain what the poet sees in the exercise of that rule.

translation: We bear witness that God descends in the darkness,
as Ahmad, sent with the truth, declared.
16.sharh: Ahmad is another name for Muhammad. The hadith invoked here connects the last third of the night with an invitation to ask and seek forgiveness.

translation: We bear witness that God sent His messengers
with His signs to lead and guide creation.
17.sharh: The signs belong to the One who sent the messengers. They authenticate the message as well as showing its hearers a way to live.

translation: He gave different ranks to messengers and to all creatures,
in His wisdom. Exalted is the Great, the One.
18.sharh: The messengers share a vocation and differ in rank. The poet places that difference within the divine wisdom already described.

translation: The best of God’s creation on earth and in heaven
is Muhammad, prophet of guidance to all worlds.
19.sharh: Muhammad’s name is held back until the end. The sweep from earth to heaven sets the scale of the honour claimed for him.

translation: The Merciful chose for him those companions
who upheld guidance and faith and prepared the way.
20.sharh: The companions’ distinction appears in what they did for later generations. The last verb pictures them making a road passable for others.

translation: To love his whole family and all his companions
is, for us who hold to truth, a binding duty.
21.sharh: Family and companions receive a single inclusive obligation. The emphasis on “all” matters to the teaching he is setting out.

translation: Those who hold to truth say that His speech
is wording and meaning together, expressed with excellence.
22.sharh: The claim concerns both what the Quran says and the particular words in which it says it. This distinction prepares the assertion about creation in the next verse.

translation: It is uncreated. How could His creatures ever
speak as God speaks, when He is more glorious?
23.sharh: “It” carries forward the speech of God. The question links its uniqueness to the difference between the Creator and those who speak as His creatures.

translation: We bear witness that good and evil alike come
by His decree. A person still strives and makes an effort.
24.sharh: The second half names two kinds of agency in a few words. Divine decree encompasses events, and a person genuinely undertakes the actions in them.

translation: Our faith is speech, deed and intention,
all three bound to goodness and obedience.
25.sharh: The qualification in the second half matters. Simply speaking, doing or intending something does not make it an act of faith.

translation: It grows through obedience and leaving what He forbids.
Disobedience certainly diminishes it and can spoil it.
26.sharh: Faith in this account has degrees. What people do and what they refrain from doing can both affect it.

translation: We affirm all the events of the Resurrection
and bear true witness to all that realm contains.
27.sharh: The “abode” is the life to come. The single expression covers rising again, giving account and receiving the outcome of judgement.

translation: Reflect on the works of the Great One and all
His vast dominions hold, so you may find your way.
28.sharh: The teacher turns from a collective confession to a direct instruction. The learner now has to look at evidence in the surrounding world.

translation: Have you seen night come in darkness
and an army of dawn follow, driving it away?
29.sharh: Dawn has the advance and momentum of an army. The ordinary alternation between darkness and light becomes a scene to watch closely.

translation: Look throughout the reaches of the sky.
Its blazing stars move to and fro.
30.sharh: The stars show a different aspect of order from the dawn. Their repeated courses can be observed across the entire sky.

translation: Does all this have a maker who directs it,
wise, all-knowing, one, without a peer?
31.sharh: Earlier questions pointed the reader towards things to look at. This question asks what their existence and order allow the reader to infer.

translation: Yes, by Him who fashioned them truly and well
and planted secrets in them, they bear witness to God.
32.sharh: He answers his own question with an oath. The things being sworn about also furnish the evidence for the answer.

translation: On earth are signs for anyone with certainty.
Signs do little for someone bent on denial.
33.sharh: The wording echoes Quran 51:20. The difference he draws lies in how observers receive the signs available to them.

translation: Within the self are signs and wonders.
Through them God the Great is known and worshipped.
34.sharh: The movement from the earth to the self also follows Quran 51:20–21. The observer becomes an instance of the very evidence being sought.

translation: The signs stand as witnesses that He
is a mighty God whose bounty never runs out.
35.sharh: Witnesses need only appear and give their testimony. In his account the visible world has already done so.

translation: Whoever belongs to God’s planting answers Him.
Whoever turns and walks away has none to help him prosper.
36.sharh: Planting introduces an image of living growth under divine care. The contrast is expressed in two movements, answering a call and turning one’s back on it.

translation: Be mindful of God by doing what He commands.
Avoid what He forbids and keep away.
37.sharh: Mindfulness takes a specific form here. It governs both the action a person undertakes and the distance they keep from a forbidden one.

translation: Be sincere towards God. Beware of showing off.
Follow God’s Messenger in your worship.
38.sharh: One test concerns the audience for whom a person acts. The other concerns the example on which the action is modelled.

translation: Trust the Merciful in earnest. Put your confidence in Him,
that He may meet your needs and you find your way.
39.sharh: Trust is paired with confidence in God’s sufficiency. Guidance concerns how a person pursues the things they need as well as whether they obtain them.

translation: Hold back from sin and bear His decrees patiently.
Persevere in obedience, that you may be happy.
40.sharh: Three forms of the same Arabic root describe restraint, endurance and perseverance. The practical demands differ even when the virtue has one name.

translation: Travel between fear and hope.
They are a bird’s two wings as you head towards your goal.
41.sharh: The point of the bird is movement towards a destination. Fear and hope work together to sustain that movement.

translation: Cleanse your heart of every ill.
Keep watching for its faults at all times.
42.sharh: The two instructions make a continuing practice. Inspection reveals a fault and enables the work of removing it.

translation: Adorn your heart by wishing people well.
That is its finest and most generous adornment.
43.sharh: The earlier work was to remove a fault. He now supplies something positive to cultivate in its place, goodwill towards others.

translation: When you choose a companion, choose one rightly guided,
who sincerely leads you towards good.
44.sharh: A good companion functions as another guide on the road of the opening verse. What matters is where their influence carries you.

translation: Beware of someone whose company
brings you an unquestionable loss.
45.sharh: A companion may impose a cost that outlasts the time spent together. This warning completes the counsel about choosing whom to follow.

translation: Take what comes readily in your companion’s character,
as the Merciful commands and teaches.
46.sharh: This echoes Quran 7:199. In dealings with friends it means accepting what people can readily give of themselves and avoiding needless exactions.

translation: Set out from this world. It is no lasting residence.
It is provisions for those who stock up.
47.sharh: The world supplies a traveller with what the next stage requires. Preparing to leave gives present conduct its particular value.

translation: Follow the paths of those who went before
to the lasting abode that never runs out.
48.sharh: The traveller has predecessors whose route can be followed. A lasting destination gives direction to the temporary journey.

translation: Remember God in every circumstance.
No fixed time confines remembrance of God.
49.sharh: Remembrance includes keeping God in mind and on the tongue. Its availability through an ordinary day is central to the instruction.

translation: Remembering the God of the Throne, privately and openly,
lifts distress and worry from you and drives them away.
50.sharh: The verbs first remove anxiety, then send it further off. Both private devotion and spoken remembrance can have this effect.

translation: It brings good here and in the life to come.
If the whisperer visits you, it drives him off.
51.sharh: The effects run in opposite directions. Remembrance draws benefits near and sends the intrusive whisperer away.

translation: The Chosen One once told his companions
that a frequent rememberer runs ahead alone.
52.sharh: Muhammad once named the people who had drawn ahead as those who remember God often. Solitude in the image is the gap a runner opens up in front.

translation: He told Mu'adh to ask his God for help
in remembering, giving thanks and worshipping well.
53.sharh: The three requests echo a prayer Muhammad taught Mu'adh ibn Jabal. Good worship itself is something for which the worshipper asks help.

translation: He also advised a man who came for counsel,
finding the burden of religious duties heavy,
54.sharh: This introduces a different conversation. A man overwhelmed by the number of observances wanted something he could hold fast to.

translation: “Let your tongue be always moist.” This practice
helps in every undertaking and brings happiness.
55.sharh: A moist tongue suggests words spoken again and again. The counsel gives the adviser’s many earlier instructions a practice that can accompany them all.

translation: He said remembrance plants something for its people
in Eden’s gardens, where homes are made ready.
56.sharh: The image gives an utterance a future life as something planted. The gardens and their dwellings belong to the world to come.

translation: He said that God remembers His servant
and is with him, setting his affairs right.
57.sharh: Remembrance now runs in both directions. Divine companionship in this verse shows itself in help towards sound judgement and action.

translation: He said remembrance continues in paradise
when obligations end and its people live there for ever.
58.sharh: The hadith behind this passage compares praise in paradise to breathing. It continues there freely once the conditions of earthly duty have ended.

translation: Even if remembering Him did nothing more
than guide the way to the love of God,
59.sharh: The poet deliberately supposes a much narrower list of benefits. The conclusion of the conditional sentence will take two more verses to arrive.

translation: and keep a person from backbiting and tale-bearing
and from every word that corrupts their religion,
60.sharh: The first offence hurts someone absent, the second carries words between people to set them at odds. The same tongue can be occupied with something else.

translation: we would have ample cause and every wish
to remember God often. How worthy is the One.
61.sharh: Even the abbreviated list would suffice. In praising God at its close he gives the reader a small instance of the practice he recommends.

translation: Yet through ignorance we remember Him so little,
as we so rarely devote ourselves to worship.
62.sharh: The teacher returns to “we”, this time to admit a shared failing. Knowing the list of benefits has yet to become the practice it commends.

translation: Ask your Lord always for help to act rightly and succeed.
No servant who turns to the Watchful One is forsaken.
63.sharh: Tawfiq is the help by which good intention becomes right action. The final divine name suggests one who watches over the servant asking for it.

translation: My God, give blessing, peace and mercy
to the best guide creation has known,
64.sharh: Having asked the reader to pray, he prays himself. The closing description of Muhammad returns to guidance, the opening concern of the poem.

translation: and to his family, companions and all who follow,
a blessing and greeting of peace that last for ever.
65.sharh: The blessing extends through the generations of those who follow. Its requested duration supplies the last word of a poem about a lasting destination.

1.1.4.head: مَنهَج
1.1.4.meaning: A clear road, used here for a course of belief and conduct.

1.2.3.head: القَوم
1.2.3.meaning: The people whose way he will describe, later called “the people of truth”.

2.1.6.head: نَظَمَ
2.1.6.meaning: To put into verse. Its first image is threading beads on a string.

4.2.3.head: ذُلّ
4.2.3.meaning: The worshipper's willing humility before God.

6.1.2.head: مَلَك
6.1.2.meaning: Angels. A less familiar plural of malak than mala'ika.

7.1.3.head: نِدّ
7.1.3.meaning: A rival set up as an equal or partner to God.

7.1.4.head: كُفء
7.1.4.meaning: Someone or something equal in standing.

8.1.2-3.head: أَخبارُ الصِّفات
8.1.2-3.meaning: What the Qur'an and transmitted reports say about the attributes of God.

8.2.3.head: تَأويل
8.2.3.meaning: Here the reinterpretation of scriptural attributes in a way the poet believes denies them.

9.1.4.head: كُنه
9.1.4.meaning: A thing's innermost reality, what it is in itself.

10.1.2.head: الصَّمَد
10.1.2.meaning: A divine name, the self-sufficient Lord to whom creatures turn in their need.

11.1.5.head: قَهر
11.1.5.meaning: Sovereign power that nothing can withstand.

12.1.3.head: القَيّوم
12.1.3.meaning: The one who subsists of himself and sustains everything else.

16.1.6.head: الدُّجى
16.1.6.meaning: The darkness of night. The report he invokes specifies its last third.

16.2.5.head: أَحمَد
16.2.5.meaning: Ahmad, another name of the Prophet Muhammad.

17.2.1.head: آيَة
17.2.1.meaning: A sign borne by a messenger, including the words of revelation he recites.

20.1.5.head: الأُلى
20.1.5.meaning: An older relative pronoun meaning “those who”.

21.1.3.head: آل
21.1.3.meaning: Here the Prophet's household, named alongside his Companions.

22.2.5.head: مُجَوَّد
22.2.5.meaning: Excellently wrought, said of the divine words and their meaning together.

23.1.3.head: أَنّى
23.1.3.meaning: “How could …?” A question that rules out the possibility.

24.2.1.head: تَقدير
24.2.1.meaning: God's decree of events in accordance with his prior knowledge.

25.2.5.head: قَيَّدَ
25.2.5.meaning: To qualify the preceding terms, here by restricting them to acts of obedience.

27.2.3.head: الدّار
27.2.3.meaning: The life to come and what it holds after resurrection.

28.1.2.head: أَثَر
28.1.2.meaning: A trace of the Creator's work from which his knowledge and power may be recognised.

30.1.2.head: رَجاً
30.1.2.meaning: A quarter or far reach. The word appears here in the plural.

31.1.3.head: مُحدِث
31.1.3.meaning: One who brings something into existence.

33.1.6.head: موقِن
33.1.6.meaning: One firmly convinced of the truth.

36.1.4.head: غَرس
36.1.4.meaning: A planting, here people cultivated in obedience as a gardener tends trees.

38.1.6.head: رِياء
38.1.6.meaning: Doing a religious act for people to see and praise. The final hamza falls away in the verse.

40.2.1.head: صابَرَ
40.2.1.meaning: To persist in patience against an ongoing difficulty.

41.1.5.head: رَجاء
41.1.5.meaning: Hope in God's mercy. Its final hamza falls away here.

43.1.2.head: نُصح
43.1.2.meaning: Sincerely desiring and seeking another person's good.

46.1.2.head: العَفو
46.1.2.meaning: What people can readily give of their character and conduct, an expression from Qur'an 7:199.

47.2.2.head: زاد
47.2.2.meaning: Provisions for a journey, a figure for deeds a person can take into the next life.

48.1.3.head: طَريق
48.1.3.meaning: Roads. The middle vowel of the plural turuq is dropped for the metre.

50.2.2.head: شَقاء
50.2.2.meaning: Misery or wretchedness. The final hamza is elided in the poem.

51.1.4.head: آجِل
51.1.4.meaning: What comes later, here the life to come.

51.2.5.head: شَرَّدَ
51.2.5.meaning: To drive far away, what remembrance does to the whisperer.

52.1.3.head: المُختار
52.1.3.meaning: The Chosen One, an epithet of Muhammad.

52.2.6.head: مُفرِد
52.2.6.meaning: One running ahead of the field. In the hadith the Prophet identifies those ahead as men and women who remember God often.

53.1.2.head: مُعاذ
53.1.2.meaning: Mu'adh ibn Jabal, the Companion whom the Prophet taught to ask for help in remembrance, gratitude and worship.

54.2.5.head: شَريعَة
54.2.5.meaning: Here the various practices and duties prescribed by religion.

56.2.2.head: عَدن
56.2.2.meaning: Lasting residence, as in the Qur'anic “gardens of lasting abode”.

57.2.5.head: سَدَّدَ
57.2.5.meaning: To guide someone to the right word or action.

58.2.2.head: تَكليف
58.2.2.meaning: The state of being bound by religious commands and prohibitions in this life.

60.1.4.head: غيبَة
60.1.4.meaning: Saying something about an absent person that they would dislike hearing, even if true.

60.1.5.head: نَميمَة
60.1.5.meaning: Carrying tales between people in a way that sets them against one another.

63.2.4.head: المُهَيمِن
63.2.4.meaning: A divine name, the Watcher and Guardian over creation.
